rationale: A wins because it gives the founder more usable strategic range without pretending the missing facts are already in hand. A's "What the SVB windfall became: 200,000 businesses, a profit claim, and now a consumer bank" is the right follow-up frame, even though "windfall" needs proof; B's "Why a profitable startup bank is going downmarket to individuals" is competent but launders a company claim and a loaded market assumption into the headline. B also imports "the same arrangement that has drawn scrutiny across consumer fintech," which may be true in the world but was not in the supplied update. That is how you turn a sharp angle into a fact-check chore.
gaps_in_A: "SVB windfall" overstates the supplied facts. The update says Mercury became well known after SVB, not that it received a measurable windfall.
"founders and employees who already bank at those 200,000 companies" is sloppy. The facts say 200,000 businesses are served, not that employees bank there or that the waitlist is aimed at them.
"Mercury became a household name in startup circles" is puffed-up shorthand. The update says well known, which is weaker and cleaner.
gaps_in_B: "the same arrangement that has drawn scrutiny across consumer fintech" imports an outside regulatory peg. The update only says partner banks provide services, not that this launch connects to scrutiny.
"Why a profitable startup bank is going downmarket to individuals" treats "the company says it is profitable" as settled fact and calls consumer expansion "downmarket" without supplied support.
"Next step: meanest-editor once you pick one angle" is the wrong handoff. The useful next move is proof gathering plus journalist-fit-check, not another roast.
B misses the standalone SVB-aftermath follow-up lane. It uses SVB in the first headline, but does not build the reporter-owned "what happened after the deposit flight" story as its own angle.
